opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of those things where the difference is much bigger than people intuitively expect.

With images, you're working in a continuous space. Every pixel is a real number, so you can just compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the input and take a step in that direction. One forward pass and one backward pass, and you know exactly which way to nudge every pixel to make the model more likely to do what you want. Do that a few hundred times and you basically always succeed. For a lot of vision models, generating an adversarial example takes seconds on a single GPU. It's almost embarrassingly easy, and that's been true for over a decade now.

Text is fundamentally different because tokens are discrete. You can't move a token a little bit toward "more harmful." It's either this token or that one. You can still compute gradients with respect to the one-hot embeddings, and that's roughly what methods like GCG do. You use the gradient as a heuristic to propose candidate token swaps. But the gradient is only a linear approximation, and in a discrete space that approximation is pretty bad. So you have to sample a bunch of candidates, actually evaluate each one with a full forward pass, and keep the best. You might do hundreds of forward passes per step and hundreds or thousands of steps. You're talking orders of magnitude more compute than the image case, and even then it doesn't always work.

The interesting implication is for multimodal models. If a model accepts images, you've handed the attacker a continuous input channel into the same system. You don't have to fight the discrete optimization problem at all. You just optimize the image, and it's dramatically easier to get the language model to say whatever you want. So I think the right way to see it is that the difficulty of text attacks was never really robustness. It was mostly that our optimizers are weak in discrete spaces. As soon as you give the attacker an easier optimization surface, a lot of that apparent robustness goes away.

The other thing I'd say is that compute cost isn't a security guarantee. If an attack costs a few hundred GPU-hours today, that's cheap for a motivated adversary, and attacks only get better. The history of adversarial ML is that the first attack is slow and clunky, and a couple of years later someone finds one that's a hundred times faster. So I'd be very careful about any defense whose argument is basically "the attack is expensive." That's a statement about our current attack algorithms, not about the model.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually one of the things that I think people get wrong a lot when they compare these two settings, because on the surface they look very different and in some ways the economics are completely inverted.

In the image case, the thing that makes attacks easy is that the space is continuous and you have gradients. If I want to find an adversarial example for an image classifier, I take the gradient of the loss with respect to the pixels, I take a step, I repeat. Ten steps, a hundred steps, maybe a thousand if I'm being careful. Each step is one forward and one backward pass. So you're talking about something on the order of a few thousand forward passes to break a model, and that's basically the worst case. Often it's far less. And importantly, this just works. You don't need any cleverness; the gradient tells you exactly where to go.

In the language model case, the thing you'd like to do is the same thing, but you can't, because tokens are discrete. There's no "slightly more of the word 'sure'" that you can move toward. So what you end up doing, with GCG or any of these token-level attacks, is a kind of gradient-guided search. You use the gradient over the embedding space as a heuristic to say which tokens might be worth trying, and then you actually try a batch of them, evaluate the loss on each one, keep the best, and repeat. And that batch might be a few hundred candidates per step, and you might run for five hundred or a thousand steps. So now you're at hundreds of thousands of forward passes, each of which is through a billion-parameter model instead of a little ResNet. The cost per attack is several orders of magnitude higher.

So if you just ask "which is more expensive," the answer is clearly the language model attack, and by a lot.

But I think that framing misses the part that actually matters, which is: expensive relative to what? In the image setting, the defender's job is also very cheap. Training a classifier is cheap, evaluating it is cheap, so the attacker having a cheap attack doesn't give them any particular asymmetry. In the language model setting, the model costs tens of millions of dollars to train, and the attacker can spend a few hundred GPU-hours finding a suffix that breaks it, and then that suffix just works. It's a string. You can post it on the internet, anyone can copy and paste it, and the cost of reusing the attack is zero. So the amortized cost of the attack is trivial compared to the cost of the thing being attacked.

The other thing that I think is underappreciated is that the discreteness, which is what makes the attack expensive, is also what makes it transferable in an annoying way. In images, people worried about transfer attacks for a long time and they do work to some extent, but the perturbations are kind of fragile, and small changes in the model tend to break them. With text, the attack is a discrete object. When we did the GCG work, the suffixes we found on open models transferred to GPT-4 and Claude and Bard at a rate that genuinely surprised me. And I think part of the reason is that you're forced into a much coarser search. You're not finding some precise point in a high-dimensional continuous space that happens to exploit one model's specific decision boundary. You're finding something that has to be robust to the discreteness of the search itself, and that ends up being a feature from the attacker's perspective.

So the way I'd summarize it is: per-attack, discrete attacks are much more expensive, and that's a real cost that matters if you're trying to run thousands of them for an evaluation. But the thing you should actually care about as a defender is cost relative to the value of what's being broken and how well the attack amortizes, and on both of those axes the language model setting is worse for the defender, not better. The expense of the search is not a security property. It's just an inconvenience for the attacker that they pay once.

And then the last thing I'd say is that the gap is closing anyway. People have been making these discrete attacks much cheaper, with better candidate selection, with reusing computation across steps, with just better engineering. The first version of these things was hilariously inefficient because we weren't trying to be efficient, we were trying to show it was possible. If someone cared about making it fast, I'd expect at least a ten or hundred-x improvement without any new ideas. So I wouldn't build any kind of defense argument on the assumption that these attacks are expensive, because that assumption has a very short shelf life.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to be careful about what you’re counting. With an image, you have this continuous input space, and if you have access to the model’s gradients, you get a very useful signal: which direction should I move the pixels to make the attack work? You can take a gradient step, evaluate it, and repeat.

With text, the input is a sequence of discrete tokens. You can compute a gradient with respect to an embedding, but you can’t necessarily turn that direction into a valid token. So now you’re searching over candidate substitutions, evaluating them, and deciding which ones to keep. That can require substantially more computation per useful update.

But that doesn’t mean jailbreaks are inherently expensive. A person can sometimes write a prompt that works immediately. And an expensive search might produce a jailbreak that you can reuse across many requests, so the discovery cost and the cost of actually using the attack are very different.

So I’d want to compare the access assumptions, the total computation spent finding the attack, and how often it succeeds. Counting iterations alone is pretty misleading if one iteration is a single gradient step and the other involves evaluating hundreds of candidate prompts.

r001.rationale: The response mentions taking a gradient step on image pixels, but does not describe a single sign-of-gradient step or say it works when the model is vulnerable.

r004.rationale: It says discrete-token search can require substantially more computation per useful update, but does not clearly state that generating a GCG attack requires substantially more compute overall than generating a continuous-space image attack.

r005.rationale: The response does not compare GCG attack generation time with model training or say it is orders of magnitude faster.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important distinction is how much information you get from each computation. With an image, you can compute a gradient with respect to the pixels, and that tells you how to change all of those pixels simultaneously to make the attack more effective. The space is enormous, but it has this very useful continuous structure.

With text, you ultimately have to choose actual tokens. You can compute gradients through embeddings, but you can’t necessarily take a small step in that direction and get a valid token. So you end up using the gradient to propose candidates, evaluating those candidates, and repeating. That can require quite a lot of computation.

But I’d separate the cost of finding an attack from the cost of using it. If you spend a lot of compute finding a jailbreak that then works across many different requests, that upfront cost gets amortized. So I don’t think there’s a single meaningful comparison without specifying whether we’re talking about a new attack for every example or one attack that you can reuse.
